query: How can we empirically dissociate apathy from depressive symptomatology: which diagnostic interviews, clinician scales, and item-level CFA/sensitivity analyses work best?

response.query: How can we empirically dissociate apathy from depressive symptomatology: which diagnostic interviews, clinician scales, and item-level CFA/sensitivity analyses work best?
response.answer: To empirically dissociate apathy from depressive symptomatology, use the Neuropsychiatric Inventory-Clinician (NPI-C) and Apathy Evaluation Scale (AES). The 16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS) can also help differentiate symptoms.

results.title: Full article: The Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology, Adolescent Version (QIDS-A17): A Psychometric Evaluation
results.content: The total CDRS-R score includes ratings of both symptoms and function, which can create a potential confound in measuring symptom remission.Citation24 Thus, the CDRS-R may be less sensitive to detecting symptom remission since the rated functional difficulties may have been present prior to MDE onset or, as in adults, they may take longer to resolve than depressive symptoms.Citation25 Further, the CDRS-R lacks a self-report version, which may be especially useful in adolescents since important symptoms of depression (an internalizing disorder) may not come to parental attention until obvious behavioral problems occur.Citation26,Citation27 Adult studies have found self-report measures can replace more time-consuming clinician-rated measures, with good correlationCitation2 and concurrent validityCitation25 established between the adult self-report and clinician-rated measures.Citation28–30. The present study evaluates the psychometric properties of each QIDS-A17 (self-report and clinician-rated) as well as the composite versions of the QIDS-A17 and the CDRS-R (each based on both the parent and adolescent clinical interviews) using classical test theory (CTT) and item response theory analyses. CTT measures of scale consistency—including Cronbach’s alpha,Citation43 item (symptom) means, total scale score means, item score-total score correlations, and intercorrelations among measures—were computed for all four depression rating scales (QIDS-A17-C(Clinician-rated on Adolescent), QIDS-A17-C (Composite, clinician-completed based on interviews with parent and child), QIDS-A17-SR (adolescent self-report), and CDRS-R (clinician-rated based on both patient and parent interview).

The Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (IDS): psychometric properties A J Rush et al. The psychometric properties of the 28- and 30-item versions of the Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology, Clinician-Rated (IDS-C) and Self-Report (IDS-SR) are reported in a total of 434 (28-item) and 337 (30-item) adult out-patients with current major depressive disorder and 118 adult euthymic subjects (15 remitted depressed and 103 normal controls). Analysis of sensitivity to change in symptom severity in an open-label trial of fluoxetine (N = 58) showed that the IDS-C and IDS-SR were highly related to the 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression. results.title: Mapping of validated apathy scales onto the apathy diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorders
results.content: For the scientific community group, 10 of 11 (90.9%) NPI-C apathy items and 7 of 18 (38.8%) AES items mapped strongly onto the DCA-NCD overall. Participants were instructed to “evaluate the extent to which items on existing apathy instruments map onto the diagnostic criteria” and that “The goal of this survey is to vote on how strongly the items on the Apathy Evaluation Scale (AES) and Neuropsychiatric Inventory-Clinician (NPI-C) apathy map onto different dimensions of the apathy diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorders.” For each item, experts and scientific community members were asked to evaluate the degree to which each item corresponded to the DCA-NCD overall and with each of the three DCA-NCD dimensions: diminished initiative (“Initiative”), diminished interest (“Interest”) and diminished emotional expression (“Emotion”). The average scores for the mapping of each item on the scale to the overall DCA-NCD were then divided by the total number of questions (11 for NPI-C apathy, and 18 for AES) on the scale for both the scales and for both the experts’ and the scientific community groups. To investigate the inter-rater reliability of both the mapping of NPI-C apathy and that of AES onto the DCA-NCD between the experts’ and the scientific community groups, Cohen’s kappa analyses were conducted. NPI-C apathy items 4 and 8 did not map globally onto the DCA-NCD (Table 100312-6/fulltext#tbl0005)). Kappa analyses showed moderate agreement between the experts and the scientific community on the mapping of both NPI-C apathy [κ (95% CI) = 0.74 (0.57, 1.00)] **(**Table 300312-6/fulltext#tbl0015)**)** and AES [κ (95% CI) = 0.63 (0.35, 1.00)] on the overall DCA-NCD (Table 400312-6/fulltext#tbl0020)). For inter-rater reliability between the experts and the scientific community for the mapping of the NPI-C apathy onto the DCA-NCD there was weak agreement [κ (95% CI) = 0.45 (0.22, 1.00)] for “Initiative,” but perfect agreement for “Interest” [κ (95% CI) = 1.00, (1.00, 1.00)] and “Emotion” (κ (95% CI) = 1.00 (1.00, 1.00)] (Table 300312-6/fulltext#tbl0015)). While both scales had items addressing the three dimensions, both groups indicated that the NPI-C apathy mapped more strongly and uniquely onto each dimension and the overall DCA-NCD compared to the AES.

results.title: Mapping of validated apathy scales onto the apathy diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorders
results.content: For the scientific community group, 10 of 11 (90.9%) NPI-C apathy items and 7 of 18 (38.8%) AES items mapped strongly onto the DCA-NCD overall. Participants were instructed to “evaluate the extent to which items on existing apathy instruments map onto the diagnostic criteria” and that “The goal of this survey is to vote on how strongly the items on the Apathy Evaluation Scale (AES) and Neuropsychiatric Inventory-Clinician (NPI-C) apathy map onto different dimensions of the apathy diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorders.” For each item, experts and scientific community members were asked to evaluate the degree to which each item corresponded to the DCA-NCD overall and with each of the three DCA-NCD dimensions: diminished initiative (“Initiative”), diminished interest (“Interest”) and diminished emotional expression (“Emotion”). The average scores for the mapping of each item on the scale to the overall DCA-NCD were then divided by the total number of questions (11 for NPI-C apathy, and 18 for AES) on the scale for both the scales and for both the experts’ and the scientific community groups. Paired t-tests were used to assess within-group differences in the mean mapping scores for NPI-C apathy and AES mapping onto the DCA-NCD, within the experts’ and the scientific community groups. To investigate the inter-rater reliability of both the mapping of NPI-C apathy and that of AES onto the DCA-NCD between the experts’ and the scientific community groups, Cohen’s kappa analyses were conducted. Experts: This group indicated 10 of 11 (90.9%) items on the NPI-C apathy mapped (mean scores > 1.5) onto one of the three dimensions of the DCA-NCD: two onto “Initiative”, six onto “Interest”, and two onto “Emotion”. Kappa analyses showed moderate agreement between the experts and the scientific community on the mapping of both NPI-C apathy [κ (95% CI) = 0.74 (0.57, 1.00)] (Table 3 ) and AES [ κ (95% CI) = 0.63 (0.35, 1.00)] on the overall DCA-NCD ( Table 4 ). Both expert and the scientific community group showed perfect agreement on NPI-C apathy items 5–10 being strongly mapped onto “Interest”. While both scales had items addressing the three dimensions, both groups indicated that the NPI-C apathy mapped more strongly and uniquely onto each dimension and the overall DCA-NCD compared to the AES.
